scenes.title: Binary search: one look at the middle, half the list gone
scenes.intent: predict which half survives each comparison, and say why sorted order makes that safe

framing.intro: Pause any time and change the target: the search recomputes, and you can watch whether the number of comparisons moves.
framing.outro: If you can say, before the animation does, which half gets thrown away — you have the idea.

citations.claim: binary search on a sorted array runs in Theta(lg n) comparisons.

scenes.title: Insertion sort: walking one card back into place
scenes.intent: connect the number of comparisons to how unordered the input was

framing.intro: Watch the comparisons, not the swaps: a value moves only while the card to its left is bigger.
framing.outro: Nearly sorted input cost you almost nothing per card. That is why this sort survives in real libraries for small ranges.

citations.claim: insertion sort runs in Theta(n) on already sorted input and Theta(n^2) worst case.

scenes.title: Gates: two wires in, one rule out
scenes.intent: predict any row of the truth table from the rule rather than from memory

framing.intro: Answer the prompt before the output frame appears. Being wrong here is the useful part.
framing.outro: NAND and NOR are functionally complete: you can build every other gate from one kind.

citations.claim: switching circuits can be described and minimised with Boolean algebra.

scenes.title: The instruction cycle, register by register
scenes.intent: name what each phase of the cycle moves, and why PC advances before execute

framing.intro: a straight line program: three fetch, decode, execute cycles, then a halt
framing.outro: Every phase in here is a register transfer. If you cannot say which register changed, that is the frame to replay.

concepts: conditional jump as a PC write

citations.claim: storing instructions and data in one memory makes a program self modifiable and the machine general.

scenes.title: A loop in the cycle: counting down to a jump
scenes.intent: name what each phase of the cycle moves, and why PC advances before execute

framing.intro: a countdown loop: it ends only when the subtraction reaches zero and the JZ sends PC past the last instruction
framing.outro: Every phase in here is a register transfer. If you cannot say which register changed, that is the frame to replay.

concepts: conditional jump as a PC write

binary_search.title: Binary search on a sorted list
binary_search.summary: Watch the search range halve at every comparison, and see why sorted order is what makes one look at the middle worth two looks at the ends.

values.label: The list
values.help: sorted, no repeats, 3 to 24 numbers. Left empty, the lesson generates one from the seed.

n.label: List size
n.help: how many values to search through

target.label: Target
target.help: the value to look for. Any number works, including one that is not in the list.

cpu_cycle.title: The CPU instruction cycle: fetch, decode, execute
cpu_cycle.summary: Step a program through a one accumulator machine and watch PC, MAR, MDR and IR take their turn in every instruction — one memory for code and data, and no way to stop but HLT.

program.label: Program
program.help: one instruction per line, up to 8: LOAD, STORE, ADD, SUB, JMP, JZ, HLT

data.label: Data cells
data.help: the numbers the program reads and writes, in cells right after the program

max_steps.label: Stop after this many instructions
max_steps.help: a loop that never ends is cut off, and says so

logic_gates.title: Logic gates: inputs, rule, output
logic_gates.summary: Drive the inputs of one gate and watch the rule decide the output, with the whole truth table beside it so you can predict the next row before it is shown.

walk.label: Walk the whole truth table
walk.help: off: only the inputs you set. on: every row, in counting order.

b.label: Input B
b.help: ignored by a single input gate

sorting.title: Insertion sort: build a sorted prefix one card at a time
sorting.summary: Watch each value get walked back into the sorted part of the list by comparison, and count how many comparisons and shifts the whole sort really costs.

values.label: The list
values.help: any order, repeats allowed — 2 to 20 numbers

body.note: every scene here was validated before it was stored: the frames are computed by the backend simulation, and a scene carries nothing to execute

opened.intent: predict which half survives each comparison, and say why sorted order makes that safe

framing.intro: Pause any time and change the target: the search recomputes, and you can watch whether the number of comparisons moves.
framing.outro: If you can say, before the animation does, which half gets thrown away — you have the idea.

citations.claim: binary search on a sorted array runs in Theta(lg n) comparisons.

frames.title: 12 sorted values, and one target
frames.narration: Looking for 37. The list is sorted, so the only thing we need to know at any moment is the range where it could still be: index 0 to 11.

prompt.question: For 12 sorted values, how many comparisons does a search like this need, worst case?

frames.title: arr[5] = 35, target 37
frames.narration: The live range is index 0 to 11. Its middle is 5, which holds 35. Because 35 is smaller than 37, the target can only be to the right.

prompt.question: arr[5] is 35 and the target is 37. Which half survives this comparison?

frames.title: half the range removed
frames.narration: arr[5] = 35 < 37, so index 5 and everything left of it is out. The range goes from 12 places to 6.
frames.cause: arr[5] = 35 < 37, so index 5 and everything left of it is out

prompt.question: With that half gone, which index gets looked at next?

frames.title: arr[8] = 44, target 37
frames.narration: The live range is index 6 to 11. Its middle is 8, which holds 44. Because 44 is larger than 37, the target can only be to the left.

prompt.question: arr[8] is 44 and the target is 37. Which half survives this comparison?

frames.title: half the range removed
frames.narration: arr[8] = 44 > 37, so index 8 and everything right of it is out. The range goes from 6 places to 2.
frames.cause: arr[8] = 44 > 37, so index 8 and everything right of it is out

prompt.question: With that half gone, which index gets looked at next?

frames.title: arr[6] = 37
frames.narration: The middle of the live range is index 6, holding 37.

frames.title: Found at index 6
frames.narration: 37 is at index 6. Every comparison in this search removed half of what was left, which is why 12 sorted values take 3 comparisons instead of up to 12 looks.

frames.title: 3 comparisons for 12 values
frames.narration: log2(12) is about 3.58, and this search used 3 comparisons. Halving is why sorted data is worth keeping.
